When someone dies, their heirs generally receive assets like stocks or a home at a stepped up cost basis, which is the value on the date of death. That means the gain that built up during the original owner's life is wiped out for income tax. If your parent bought stock for 10,000 dollars and it is worth 100,000 when you inherit, your new basis is 100,000. You could sell it with little or no capital gains tax. topics.title: A Non-Working Spouse Can Still Have An IRA: Here's How
tags: retirement for stay at home parent
topics.script: A spouse with no income can still save for retirement. It is called a spousal IRA. If you file a joint return, the working spouse's income can cover contributions for both. For 2026, that means up to 7,500 dollars in each spouse's IRA, or 8,600 if 50 or older, as long as the couple's total earned income covers the contributions. Traditional IRA contributions may be deductible, depending on income and workplace plan coverage, and Roth contributions grow tax free. It is a smart way for stay at home parents to build their own retirement savings. Confirm eligibility on irs.gov.

topics.title: Low-Income Year? That's The Best Time To Do A Roth Conversion
topics.script: A year when your income dips can be a golden opportunity. Maybe you changed jobs, took time off, or just retired before Social Security begins. In a low income year, you can convert money from a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA and pay tax at lower rates. For 2026, the 12 percent bracket goes up to about 50,400 dollars of taxable income for single filers, and 100,800 for married couples. Once the money is in the Roth, future growth and qualified withdrawals are tax free, and there are no required minimum distributions. Watch your total income, and talk to a tax professional.

topics.title: Work For Tips? You May Deduct Up To $25,000 From 2025 Through 2028
topics.script: If you earn tips, there is a big new deduction to know. For tax years 2025 through 2028, you can deduct up to 25,000 dollars of qualified tips from your taxable income. The deduction starts to phase out above 150,000 dollars of income, or 300,000 for joint filers. Your job has to be on the IRS list of occupations that customarily receive tips, and the tips must be reported on your W 2, 1099, or Form 4137. You need a Social Security number, and married couples must file jointly. Keep records of your tips, and check the IRS guidance at irs.gov.

topics.title: Age 65 Or Older? Claim An Extra $6,000 Deduction
topics.script: If you are 65 or older, there is a new tax break for you. For tax years 2025 through 2028, you can claim an extra 6,000 dollar deduction, 12,000 for a married couple where both spouses qualify. It comes on top of the regular standard deduction and the extra deduction for age 65 and over. The deduction starts to phase out when your income goes over 75,000 dollars, or 150,000 for joint filers. You must have a Social Security number and, if married, file jointly. You can claim it even if you take the standard deduction. Confirm the details on irs.gov.

topics.title: Work Overtime? Deduct Up To $12,500 Of It
topics.script: If you work overtime, you may get a new deduction. For tax years 2025 through 2028, you can deduct up to 12,500 dollars of qualified overtime pay, or 25,000 for joint filers. Here is the catch. Only the extra half of time and a half counts, the premium part that federal law requires. It starts phasing out above 150,000 dollars of income, or 300,000 for joint filers. The overtime must be reported on your W 2 or another statement from your employer. You also need a Social Security number. Check your pay stubs for the overtime premium, and confirm details at irs.gov.
